scenes.narration: In 1814, a tsunami of beer flooded the streets of London.
At the Horse Shoe Brewery, a huge vat of beer burst and set off a chain reaction with the other vats.
More than one million liters of beer exploded out, smashing walls and flooding the poor houses nearby.
Eight people died. Legend says crowds rushed to scoop up the free beer, but historians say that story may be exaggerated.
The brewery was found not guilty. It was called an act of God. Would you have grabbed a cup?

caption: A beer tsunami hit London in 1814. This is not a joke.

on_screen_title: HE LOST HIS NOSE OVER MATH

scenes.narration: A famous astronomer lost his nose in a duel over math.
In 1566, Danish nobleman Tycho Brahe reportedly fought his cousin over a mathematical formula. A sword sliced off part of his nose.
For the rest of his life he wore a metal nose, and analysis of his remains showed it was made of brass.
It gets weirder. He reportedly had a pet moose that drank too much beer at a party, fell down the stairs, and died.
Yet this man mapped the stars more precisely than anyone before the telescope. Genius or madman?

caption: Metal nose, a party moose, and the most precise star maps of his time.

on_screen_title: A POPE PUT A CORPSE ON TRIAL

scenes.narration: In 897, a pope dug up the body of the previous pope and put him on trial.
Pope Stephen the Sixth had the corpse of Pope Formosus dressed in papal robes and seated on a throne.
A deacon stood next to the body and answered the questions for the dead man.
scenes.image_query: Le Pape Formose et Etienne VII

scenes.narration: The corpse was found guilty. They cut off the fingers he used for blessings and threw the body into the Tiber river.
Months later, Stephen himself was thrown in prison and strangled. Is this the strangest trial in history?

caption: The trial of a dead pope. Yes, the defendant was a corpse.

scenes.narration: In 1962, a laughing epidemic shut down schools in Africa.
It started at a girls' boarding school in Kashasha, in what is now Tanzania, when three students began laughing and couldn't stop.
It spread to dozens of students, then to nearby villages. The attacks could last hours, with crying and fainting.
Around a thousand people were affected, and more than a dozen schools had to close. It went on for many months.
Experts believe it was mass psychogenic illness, triggered by stress. Have you ever been unable to stop laughing?

caption: Laughter really can be contagious. In 1962 it closed schools.

scenes.narration: In 1618, two officials were thrown out of a castle window, and it started a thirty year war.
Angry Protestant nobles in Prague grabbed two Catholic royal officials and their secretary and threw them out of a window about twenty meters high.
Amazingly, all three survived. Catholics said angels caught them. Protestants later claimed they landed in a pile of manure.
But the incident lit the fuse for the Thirty Years' War, one of the deadliest conflicts in European history, with millions dead.
Fun fact: the word defenestration means throwing someone out of a window. Angels or manure?

caption: A window, three officials, and one of Europe's deadliest wars.

scenes.narration: In 1858, London smelled so bad that Parliament almost fled the city.
For years, Londoners dumped their sewage straight into the River Thames. Then came a hot summer.
The river baked in the heat, and the smell became so horrible that people called it The Great Stink.
Parliament hung curtains soaked in chemicals to block the stench. Members of Parliament reportedly covered their faces with handkerchiefs.
Finally, they approved a giant sewer system that London still uses today. Would you have survived the smell?

caption: It took an unbearable stink to give London its sewers.

scenes.narration: A Japanese soldier kept fighting World War Two until 1974.
In 1944, Lieutenant Hiroo Onoda was sent to Lubang Island in the Philippines with orders to never surrender.
The war ended in 1945, but he believed the leaflets announcing it were enemy tricks. He hid in the jungle for decades.
In 1974, a young Japanese traveler found him. Onoda still refused to give up unless his commander ordered it.
So Japan flew his old commander to the island to officially relieve him. Twenty nine years. Loyalty or tragedy?

caption: The war ended in 1945. For him, it ended in 1974.

scenes.narration: In 1945, a chicken lived for eighteen months without its head.
A farmer in Colorado chopped off the rooster's head for dinner, but the axe missed most of the brain stem.
Mike kept walking, tried to peck for food, and even attempted to crow.
The farmer fed him with an eyedropper and took him on tour. People paid to see the headless wonder chicken.
Today his hometown celebrates a festival in his honor. Would you pay to see Mike?

caption: Mike lost his head in 1945 and kept going for 18 months.

on_screen_title: AN IRON BAR THROUGH HIS HEAD

scenes.narration: In 1848, an iron bar shot straight through a man's skull, and he survived.
Phineas Gage was building a railroad in Vermont when an explosion launched a meter long iron rod through his head.
It entered under his left cheek and flew out the top of his skull. Minutes later, he was talking.
But friends said his personality changed so much that he was, in their words, no longer Gage.
His case taught doctors that parts of the brain shape who we are. Could you survive that?

caption: He survived an iron rod through the brain and changed neuroscience.

topic: Victor Lustig sold the Eiffel Tower

scenes.narration: In 1925, a con man sold the Eiffel Tower. Twice, reportedly.
Victor Lustig read that the tower was expensive to maintain. So he posed as a government official.
He invited scrap metal dealers to a fancy hotel and told them, in secret, that Paris would sell the tower for scrap.
A dealer named André Poisson paid him. Then Lustig fled. Poisson was too embarrassed to go to the police.
Lustig reportedly came back and tried the same trick again. Would you have fallen for it?

caption: The greatest con of all time? He sold the Eiffel Tower for scrap.

scenes.narration: In medieval Europe, animals were put on trial. With real lawyers.
In 1386, in Falaise, France, a pig attacked a child. The pig was arrested, tried and sentenced to death.
According to accounts, it was even dressed in human clothes for its execution.
Rats were also put on trial. One lawyer defended rats in Autun, arguing they couldn't come to court because of the cats along the way.
Courts treated animals as if they could commit crimes. Which animal would you put on trial?

caption: Pigs, rats and insects all had their day in court.

scenes.narration: Thousands died in a battle that is remembered for a wooden bucket.
In 1325, the Italian cities of Modena and Bologna fought at Zappolino, in one of the biggest battles of medieval Italy.
Modena won. Their soldiers chased the enemy to Bologna's gates and stole a bucket from a city well as a trophy.
Legend says the whole war started over that bucket. It didn't, but the name stuck: the War of the Bucket.
The bucket is still kept in Modena today. Was it worth it?

caption: Modena still keeps the bucket it stole in 1325.

scenes.narration: The shortest war in history lasted about thirty eight minutes.
In 1896, the sultan of Zanzibar died, and Khalid bin Barghash took power without Britain's approval.
Britain sent an ultimatum: leave the palace by nine in the morning. He refused.
At nine o'clock, British warships opened fire. Within forty minutes the palace was in ruins and the war was over.
Hundreds of Zanzibari fighters were killed or wounded. On the British side, one sailor was injured. Could you name a shorter war?

caption: Start to finish in under an hour. The shortest war ever recorded.

scenes.narration: For centuries, Europeans ate ground up mummies as medicine.
Doctors believed powdered mummy, called mumia, could cure everything from headaches to internal bleeding.
Demand was so high that some dealers sold fake mummies made from the bodies of executed criminals.
King Charles the Second of England reportedly took drops made from distilled human skull.
And blood from executions was sold as a cure for epilepsy. Which old remedy is the worst?

caption: Mummy powder was once sold in European pharmacies. Seriously.

scenes.narration: One of the most powerful jobs in Tudor England was helping the king on the toilet.
The Groom of the Stool attended King Henry the Eighth while he relieved himself, and helped with his hygiene.
It sounds awful, but it meant private time with the king, every single day.
So the job went to nobles, who became trusted advisers and controlled who could see the king.
The title survived in the royal household for centuries. Would you take this job for that much power?

caption: The most intimate job in the royal court was also one of the most powerful.

on_screen_title: THE BIGGEST BLAST BEFORE THE A-BOMB

scenes.narration: In 1917, a ship explosion flattened part of a Canadian city.
In Halifax harbor, the French ship Mont-Blanc, packed with explosives, collided with another ship, the Imo.
It caught fire. Crowds gathered to watch. Then it exploded, in the largest human made blast before the atomic bomb.
Nearly two thousand people died. The ship's anchor shaft was thrown more than three kilometers away.
The next day, a blizzard hit the ruined city. Had you heard of this disaster before?

caption: One collision, one burning ship, and a blast felt hundreds of kilometers away.

scenes.narration: In 1726, a woman convinced England's doctors she was giving birth to rabbits.
Mary Toft of Godalming claimed she had delivered rabbit parts, again and again.
Surgeons came to see for themselves, including a surgeon from the king's own household. Some of them believed her.
The story became a national sensation, until a doctor threatened her with a painful operation. She confessed.
The doctors who fell for it became the joke of the country. How did they believe this?

caption: One of the wildest medical hoaxes ever fooled royal surgeons.

scenes.narration: Young women were told to lick brushes covered in radioactive paint.
In the 1910s and 20s, factory workers painted glowing watch dials with radium paint.
To keep the brushes sharp, they were taught: lip, dip, paint. Some even painted their teeth to glow for fun.
Then their bones began to crumble. Many developed horrible jaw damage, and many died.
Their lawsuits helped create workplace safety rules. Had you heard their story?

caption: The women who glowed in the dark and fought back.

scenes.narration: A millionaire drank radioactive water every day as a health drink.
Eben Byers, a rich American golf champion, started drinking Radithor, water with dissolved radium, after an injury.
He reportedly drank around fourteen hundred bottles over a few years.
The radium destroyed his bones. Parts of his jaw had to be removed. He died in 1932.
A newspaper headline said: the radium water worked fine until his jaw came off. Which health trend scares you?

caption: The health drink that was literally radioactive.

scenes.narration: One man had the hiccups for sixty eight years.
In 1922, Charles Osborne from Iowa was lifting a pig for slaughter when the hiccups started.
They never stopped. Early on he hiccuped about forty times a minute.
He still married, had eight children, and lived a normal life. Guinness listed it as the longest attack of hiccups ever.
In 1990, they suddenly stopped. He died about a year later. What's your best hiccup cure?

caption: Hiccups from 1922 to 1990. A world record nobody wants.

topic: Violet Jessop survived three ship disasters
on_screen_title: SHE SURVIVED THE TITANIC... AND MORE

scenes.narration: One woman survived the Titanic and two more disasters on its sister ships.
In 1911, stewardess Violet Jessop was aboard the Olympic when it collided with a warship. It made it back to port.
In 1912 she was on the Titanic. She survived in lifeboat sixteen.
In 1916, she worked on the hospital ship Britannic. It hit a mine. She jumped, was pulled under, and hit her head, but survived again.
People called her Miss Unsinkable. Would you have stepped on another ship?

caption: Olympic, Titanic, Britannic. She was on all three.

topic: Tsutomu Yamaguchi survived two atomic bombs

scenes.narration: One man survived both atomic bombs.
Tsutomu Yamaguchi was in Hiroshima on a business trip on August sixth, 1945, when the first bomb exploded.
Badly burned, he went home to Nagasaki and returned to work.
Three days later, while describing the blast to his boss, the second bomb hit Nagasaki. He survived again.
He lived until 2010, aged ninety three, and spoke against nuclear weapons. Luckiest or unluckiest man ever?

caption: Hiroshima, then Nagasaki, three days apart. He lived to 93.

scenes.narration: In 1816, summer never came.
A year earlier, Mount Tambora in Indonesia erupted, one of the biggest eruptions in recorded history.
Its ash spread around the planet and cooled it. In New England it snowed in June.
Crops failed across Europe and North America, and famine followed.
Stuck indoors on a rainy summer at Lake Geneva, Mary Shelley started writing Frankenstein. What would you have done?

caption: A volcano, snow in June, and the birth of Frankenstein.

scenes.narration: A Roman emperor reportedly wanted to make his horse a consul.
Caligula's favorite horse was named Incitatus. According to ancient writers, it had a marble stable and an ivory manger.
It reportedly wore purple blankets and a collar of precious stones, and even had its own servants.
The historian Suetonius wrote that Caligula planned to make the horse a consul, one of the highest offices in Rome.
Many historians think it was a joke to insult the senators. Madness or trolling?

caption: Did Caligula really want his horse in government?

scenes.narration: In eighteenth century France lived a man who could not stop eating.
Tarrare could swallow huge meals, live animals and even stones. He performed his eating as a street show.
The French army tried to use him as a spy. He swallowed a box with a secret message to carry across enemy lines. He was caught.
Doctors tried to cure him, but he stayed hungry. Dark rumors followed him at the hospital.
He died in 1798. Doctors still can't explain his condition. What do you think was wrong with him?

caption: A human mystery from 18th century France: the man who could never feel full.

scenes.narration: In 1859, America and Britain nearly went to war over a pig.
On San Juan Island, both countries claimed the land. An American farmer found a pig eating his potatoes and shot it.
The pig belonged to a British company worker. The argument escalated fast.
scenes.image_query: Hudson's Bay Company Belle Vue farm

scenes.narration: Soon hundreds of American soldiers faced British warships with thousands of men. But no one fired.
The only casualty was the pig. The dispute was settled years later by the German Kaiser. Who should pay for the pig?

caption: Soldiers, warships and a standoff. The only victim: one pig.

scenes.narration: In 1876, it rained meat in Kentucky.
In Bath County, flakes of red meat fell from a clear sky over a farm.
The pieces were a few centimeters wide. Two men reportedly tasted it and said it was like mutton or venison.
Scientists examined samples. The most popular explanation: a flock of vultures vomited their food while flying.
Newspapers loved it. Would you have tasted it?

caption: Meat fell from a clear sky. The explanation is even worse.
